1a65638330: A small job of ours (<1/> in the repository) runs every hour. It reads each feed below from its publisher and keeps a copy on this site, which is why a visitor whose address a publisher refuses still sees the satellites. Your browser reads <2>our copy first</2>, and shows it at once. It asks the publisher itself only when our copy is older than the time it promised, or when there is none; a newer answer then replaces it. If the job could not reach a publisher, we go on showing the last good copy from it, with its age, until a newer one arrives: a failed read never replaces good data with an error. If neither our copy nor the publisher can be reached, the browser shows the copy it kept from your last visit. A few publishers do not let a page on another site read them at all, or their terms say a visitor's browser must not; for those our copy is the only way, and without it the app says it could not look.

a1f34ca349: Everything drawn is measured, modelled or illustrative, and says which. This page says what each word means and what we do when we are wrong.
9b15ab95a3: <1>measured</1> A position worked out from a publisher's data of a stated age: a satellite from its orbital elements, a planet from the ephemeris. The age is part of the number, and a card says "Position propagated from elements {n1} days old".
fd78a202da: <1>modelled</1> Computed from physics or a fitted orbit, with the error measured where we could: a probe's orbit continued from its last published state, the habitable zone of a star, the temperature of a bare ball at some distance.
485c7e3703: <1>illustrative</1> A picture built to explain: the spiral of the Milky Way, a procedural satellite shape, the colour of a planet nobody has seen.
63a4c36d67: Nobody has seen the surface of a planet of another star. What is known is its size, its orbit, sometimes its mass, and by which method it was found. So on every exoplanet page the size, the period and the method are the Archive's (NASA Exoplanet Archive), anything we work out is marked computed, and <1>the picture is an artist's impression</1>: its colour, clouds and land are imagined, said on the page and printed on the share picture. "Habitable zone" is said only for the band we compute (Kopparapu et al. {n1}) and always with the word computed; it says where liquid water could be possible on a rocky world's surface, never that anything lives there.
3d26f7ec8f: Where a number can be wrong
58e96e4f2d: A satellite's position is as old as its elements. After a week a low satellite such as the station can be minutes of travel from where the map draws it.
3bab61ba0d: Distances and sizes are sometimes changed so that a thing can be seen at all (satellites are drawn larger than life); the card or the picture says so.
9be6e6ca06: Where we could not look, the card says "could not look" or leaves the line out. A guess is never shown as a reading.
191992cbec: Tell us with <1>the form for a wrong number, name or position</1> on GitHub (it needs a free GitHub account). Getting it right matters more to this project than anything else. <2>There is no separate corrections log yet.</2> What exists is the project's public history: <3>the changelog</3>, which records changes of facts under its fixes, and every commit and issue on <4>GitHub</4>. e58e4261a8: Privacy: what Space Radar keeps, and what it never does
5a2865ea43: What Space Radar's free email updates keep and why, how to leave in one click, and the rest of the promise: no tracking, no cookies, no analytics.
699708954a: Space Radar has no account, no advertising, no tracker, no cookie and no analytics. Beyond the hosting's short-lived access logs (below), the only thing it keeps about anyone is an email address, and only for a person who asks for the free email updates and confirms it.
19f58dd8c3: There is nothing to sign in to, and no page sets a cookie.
b90773e404: There is no analytics script, no advertising, no tracking pixel and no social-media widget. Nothing from another company loads on these pages until you click it.
f614fee65c: The map keeps your own choices, such as a city you picked and a few display settings, in your browser's storage on your device. They are not sent to us.
8980f5ae53: Some layers of the map ask a public data service for fresh numbers, for example NASA's picture of today's clouds. Your browser makes that request, as it would to open their page. Every source is on <1>the Sources page</1>.
f052d04eb0: The pages are served by Amazon CloudFront, which keeps standard access logs: for each request, the network (IP) address, the page asked for, the time and the browser's name. They are kept for {n1} days, privately, for security and to fix faults, and then deleted. We do not use them to track or profile anyone, they hold no cookie, and nothing in them is linked to a subscription.
de5456d12e: If you subscribe, one record is kept for your address. It holds:
ce9131e5ee: the lists you picked: Space Radar news, the Journal, space games (or one game's own list), sky alerts, Space Radar models, Space Radar video;
aca660e9b2: your consent: when you asked, when you confirmed, the page you signed up on (its address without anything after a <1/>) and the version of this page you agreed to;
62ba2cd148: a short history of those steps (asked, confirmed, changed, left), so we can show that you asked;
566e251baa: a random number that makes the links in your mails work, and stops working when you leave.
834d98ddbc: It holds no name, no IP address, no location, and nothing about whether you opened a mail or clicked a link. We could not know: <1>our mails have no tracking pixel and no image, and no link in them is rewritten</1>.
5d3e39a768: To send you what you asked for, and nothing else, and to be able to show that you asked. Nobody else gets the list: it is not sold, shared or used for advertising.
b306701d65: How it works, and how to leave
0f8557abf4: <1>Double opt-in.</1> After you sign up we send one mail with a button. Nothing more is sent until you press it, and a request that is not confirmed is deleted after {n1} hours.
8aac4ad926: <1>One-click unsubscribe.</1> Every mail has an Unsubscribe link, and the List-Unsubscribe header that mail apps read for their own Unsubscribe button. No login, no survey, no "are you sure" page that asks twice.
8e3fa27cb2: <1>Preferences.</1> Every mail links to a page where you change your lists; choosing none unsubscribes you.
934f4eded7: <1>Erasure.</1> That page also has an Erase button, which deletes your record at once.
4b1792e118: While you are subscribed, the record stays.
8d04dbfb0e: When you unsubscribe (or a mail to you bounces for good, or is marked as spam), your lists are emptied, every link in your old mails stops working, and the record is deleted {n1} days later.
5f9d116a03: When you erase it, it is deleted at once. The database's own backups age out within {n1} days.
c6eee9e420: To stop abuse, the service counts sign-up attempts per network for an hour or a day. It keeps a one-way, keyed scramble of the address (a hash it cannot turn back), never the address itself, and each count is deleted when its hour or day is over.
b34c73b87f: Who sends it, and who is responsible
a9df8887a1: The mail is sent through <1>Amazon SES</1>, and the record is kept in Amazon DynamoDB, both in Amazon Web Services' EU (Stockholm) region. Amazon processes them for us, as our service provider. Like every sender on SES, an address whose mail bounces for good or is reported as spam is also kept on Amazon's own list of addresses not to mail.
01bc6c1a70: The controller of this data is the maintainer of the Space Radar project. 776fdaee33: Why a satellite's shape matters on a map
ecd6a14cb9: A map of orbits is mostly dots, and the question a visitor asks of a dot is what it is. A generic shape answers that badly: it says "satellite" for an object that may be a weather station, a spy camera or a discarded fuel tank. The shape tells you the job.
15d5bad58d: MUOS is a clear case. It is one of the US Navy's narrowband communications satellites, and it is known by its two large gold mesh reflectors. WorldView-{n1} is built round its telescope, a barrel with its aperture to the Earth under the bus. Meteosat-{n2}, the first imager of Meteosat Third Generation, is stabilised on three axes, so it no longer needs to spin as the older Meteosats do, and its box shape shows it.
e77b62d5b5: MUOS in orbit: a central body, two strings of blue solar panels and a large gold mesh dish.
3dccead29d: MUOS, close lens: a gold mesh reflector, the mark of the craft, .
284c3eb595: The stages are a different kind of object. They are not working craft. They are what was left in orbit after the launch, and on the map they now look like empty tanks with an engine at one end.
a0e1675343: Meteosat-{n1} in orbit, a foil-covered box with its round imager window and a single solar wing.
55e043b99a: Meteosat-{n1} (MTG-I1), close lens, built here from cited dimensions. It wore the generic shape before 1.4.0.
cbc24aa11c: Most of these craft have no published model. For WorldView-{n1} a search of NASA's 3D Resources, {n2} paths read on {n3}-{n4}-{n5}, found none, and no operator was found publishing one under a free licence. So the shapes are built here in code, one script a craft, from a part library first made for release 1.3.0, with the dimensions cited and the pictures listed beside each file. No image-to-3D tool was used and no published mesh was copied. The rocket stages came from a parametric builder, where one stage is a few dozen calls with its published dimensions as the arguments. SWAS is the exception in its group, from NASA's own model.
0bc78ec6de: A builder often has only a maker's illustration, a pre-launch picture and a table of sizes. The rule was to draw only what has been officially released. Military craft are drawn only from what the services and the makers have published. ViaSat-{n1} is drawn as it was designed, because no free picture shows how the first one's reflector really lies, and the card says so. The first craft's reflector did not deploy fully in {n2}, and a confident drawing of how it lies would be a claim nobody can check.

78f6823c76: Clusters became stars you can fly among in release 1.2.0, and two new trips take the same idea out to the edge of the universe we can see.
6dd7b02d21: Inside Omega Centauri: thousands of stars of many colours around a bright core.
f210902ec1: Inside Omega Centauri, {n1} light-years away: each point is one plausible star of a model built from the cluster's catalogued size.
0ef2fcda7c: A cluster used to be a smudge on the map: a glow with a label. Release 1.2.0 turned clusters into stars you can fly among, then took the same idea outward, to clusters of galaxies and to the edge of everything we can see. Along the way it added two journeys and a way to find your path home. Here is what each of them draws, and what it only suggests.
64a5b3067b: Globular clusters: a model of a kind
7d6fc5f37c: All {n1} globular clusters on the map are now drawn as stars. The numbers come from one catalogue, Harris's {n2} list: each cluster's core radius and how concentrated it is, which together give a core and an edge in light-years. The stars are placed with King's {n3} formula for how such a ball thins out, dense in the core and fading to nothing at the edge.
c3c4abcfc0: What the map does not know is where each star is. So the positions, the number of stars shown and their brightnesses are a model, seeded by the cluster's name so that every visit draws the same stars. The colours are illustrative. A point is "one plausible giant", never a stand-in for a thousand stars, so from inside the outskirts you see what that many giants would make, not a wall of light. The glow of the fainter stars no point stands for is dimmed by exactly the light the points add.
587fe8543a: Fly into Omega Centauri, {n1} light-years away and about {n2} across, and you will be inside a model of its kind. The card says "How we know: illustration".
4edcb18cbc: Open clusters are different. For {n1} of them the map draws real stars: the members that Gaia measured, from the Hunt and Reffert {n2} census, kept when their membership probability is at least one half. That is {n3} stars in all. Each keeps its measured direction on the sky. Its depth comes from its own parallax when that is precise enough, and otherwise from a seeded draw inside the cluster's measured size; the data says which, star by star. Nothing moves: no proper motion is drawn.

169c81ecbf: The Pleiades, the Hyades, the Beehive and the Southern Pleiades were already there, because their brightest stars are in the catalogue the map ships. The new stars fill in the fainter ones. Gaia's data carries a non-commercial licence (CC BY-NC {n1} IGO) and the credits page says so.
9d324000b2: Clusters of galaxies and two quasars
d1476c7516: One step out, Virgo, Coma, Fornax and Perseus are drawn as swarms of their own galaxies: {n1} of them, from VizieR tables and the Sloan Digital Sky Survey. Where a cluster's mean distance was measured from surface-brightness fluctuations, as for Virgo and Fornax, so was the spread in depth. For Coma and Perseus the depth is modelled from the spread on the sky, "because a cluster is round", and the registry says that this is an assumption.

5fb8f91d0d: The Coma Cluster as a swarm of its member galaxies.

f6f4a28079: <1>Across the Local Group</1> stops at the Milky Way seen from outside (a model: nobody has left it to look back), the Large Magellanic Cloud, Andromeda, Triangulum, and then the Local Group among {n1} neighbours. <2>Out to the edge of the universe we can see</2> goes on from the local volume to the quasar TON {n2}, to the places the first galaxies are now (none is drawn), and to the oldest light. fef341408b: From about {n1} billion light-years out the map paints WMAP's nine-year picture of the cosmic microwave background on the inside of a sphere {n2} billion light-years away, just within the horizon, with a colour scale in microkelvin. The map says that on screen, and a screen reader is given the same words. The ladder of scales now ends on a rung called Edge. d59f5fa52b: Release 1.2.0 went back to the nearest worlds and drew them more honestly: real shadows, rings as dark as they are, and plumes only where a spacecraft saw them.
ce5f48e7cd: The floor of Tycho crater and its walls, lit from a low Sun with long shadows.

2238d641b4: The Solar System was the first thing Space Radar drew, and release 1.2.0 went back to it with one question: what would an honest picture of these places show that ours did not? The answer was shadows, rings that are as dark as they really are, and plumes drawn only where a spacecraft saw them.
23bb767b3d: The Moon, at a low Sun
df5eda2ff3: The Moon looks flat at noon and wild near the terminator, where the Sun is low and every rim throws a long shadow. The map now draws those shadows. They are cast by the Moon's own heights, from LOLA, the laser altimeter on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, one height every {n1} metres at best, at the true scale of the ground. That is also the limit: a crater under about two kilometres casts no shadow, and the card says so.
8b79c5a1e1: Fly low over a crater such as Tycho or Copernicus when the Sun there is a few degrees up, and the rims and central peaks throw the shadows an orbiting camera would record. The heights are measured; the Sun is where it really is on the clock.
9e213277e6: The Taurus-Littrow valley with the Apollo {n1} lunar module and a thin line of the traverse.
784b936b2e: Apollo {n1}'s landing site in Taurus-Littrow, with the astronauts' traverse drawn on the ground.
c7fa6123f5: Two sites also carry the paths the astronauts and their rovers took. The Apollo {n1} and {n2} traverses are drawn as the Phil Stooke of the University of Western Ontario traced them, from tracks in LROC pictures and from the crews' own photographs and descriptions. Only paths with a documentary source are drawn; the others are left off rather than guessed.
2e4a1c096f: Close up, the half that faces the Earth now wears the newest picture from NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory, in the {n1} angstrom channel, which shows gas near a million degrees. It is a browse picture, a small JPEG, and the card says so. It is dated and credited, and it turns with the Sun after it was taken. The far side, which no picture saw, is drawn in the same colours. The coronal loops are written but switched off in 1.2.0.
468bdc5300: On the International Space Station, the light reddens at orbital sunrise: sunlight reddened by the air it grazes, from Rayleigh scattering only. That one is modelled and the card says so.
9b03b312a3: The giants' rings, as dark as they are
2a3faec8ef: For years the rings of Uranus were drawn as pale grey, far brighter than they are. NASA's ring fact sheet gives their albedo as about {n1} thousandths, against {n2} for the planet. Space Radar now draws them at that darkness, a thirtieth of the clouds, so that in front of the planet they are dark threads. Their radii are measured; they are drawn ten times wider than they are, so that they can be seen at all, and the Deep exposure lifts them four times, as a long exposure does in Voyager's and Keck's pictures. Neptune's rings are beside them.

1cc57a1a89: Jupiter's ring is fainter still: a halo and a main ring of dust, stopping a few millionths of the light. They are drawn from the distances and optical depths in NASA's fact sheet, and the two gossamer rings beyond are left out. Seen with the Sun behind them they show, as they did to Galileo and New Horizons; to show at all they are lifted, and the card says by how much. The Great Red Spot sits where the JUPOS team measured it, with the date on Jupiter's card.

21af0af170: Until now every model went through a "toon" ramp: three flat steps of light, whatever the surface. Gold blanket, bare aluminium, white cloth and cells under glass all came out as one flat tone with a single highlight. The turning point was SLIM, the Japanese Moon lander, rebuilt with every feature JAXA's own model shows, which still read as a yellow box.

a096728966: Galaxies and nebulae in 3D from their own numbers
3d58657854: Release 1.3.0 draws five galaxies from the numbers astronomers have published about their shape, and puts Carina and the Small Magellanic Cloud into depth.
ef6c72ed6d: The Sombrero Galaxy edge-on as a model: a round glowing bulge cut by a thin dark lane.
657200eb15: The Sombrero Galaxy as the map draws it from published numbers: a huge bulge, a thin disc, and a lane of dust seen edge-on. {n1} million light-years away.
3d959745db: A photograph of a galaxy is a single view. Hubble can show you the Sombrero as it looks from here, and nobody can show you what it looks like from above. Release 1.3.0 draws five of them as objects with a front and a back, from numbers that astronomers have published about their shape, then lets you fly round them. It also redraws one of the sky's best-known nebulae and puts the Small Magellanic Cloud into depth.
f2d0f3a83a: Each galaxy comes from one generator, which turns a short list of numbers into stars: a bulge, a disc, arms with a pitch angle, a tilt. Every number in a galaxy's registry file is tagged. It is <1>published</1> (with the paper and the page it was read from), <2>assumed</2>, or <3>illustrative</3>. From our side of a galaxy you see the photograph; turn away and the model takes over, and a slider on the card moves between the two.
6c96400a5e: Lengths are worked out at each galaxy's distance, so the size on the sky stays the measured one whatever the distance does.
bd66da54bf: The Sombrero Galaxy (M104) is {n1} million light-years away. Its model has a huge bulge of old stars (a Sersic index of {n2} and a {n3}-kiloparsec half-light radius, from Gadotti's {n4} fit), a thin disc seen almost edge-on, and the dust ring in front. The bulge is drawn round from every side. No source says which edge of the disc is nearer to us, so the sign of the tilt is assumed, and the registry says that.

b9ee82a593: M51 is a two-armed spiral seen nearly face-on, and the model draws it from its published tilt and structure. Its companion, NGC {n1}, is drawn behind it, because M51's outer arm absorbs light in front of the companion's nucleus (Ritchey and others, {n2}). How far behind, {n3} kiloparsecs, is illustrative, and so are the companion's profile and the arm that runs to it.
16918b8141: The Whirlpool Galaxy as a model seen face-on: a spiral of two arms around a bright core.
d54f83cf67: The Whirlpool Galaxy as a model, {n1} million light-years away: two arms, a bulge and a disc.

a3ab8b009c: The Antennae are two galaxies in collision, drawn as a system: each galaxy has its own frame and each tail is a stream of its parent galaxy. The tilts are read from the catalogue's outlines, but the collision has bent both galaxies, so those numbers are illustrative; how far each part of the tail is in front of or behind the rest is a model after published simulations. The distance, {n1} million light-years, is Schweizer and colleagues' ({n2}).
da7ceedb30: The Antennae galaxies as a model: two bright cores and long curved tails of stars.

08120c78e6: The Carina Nebula sits {n1} light-years away, not the {n2} an infobox gives: the Homunculus nebula's expansion parallax and Gaia's measurements of the clusters' stars agree on {n3} kiloparsecs. Its model is a bipolar cavity of two lobes about {n4} parsecs across, which Nathan Smith and colleagues described in {n5}, with a dark V-shaped lane of dust in front of the glowing gas and Eta Carinae inside it. Fourteen hot O and Wolf-Rayet stars sit at the places SIMBAD gives. The depth of the glowing wall is not measured, and the card says so.
98e509415b: The Small Magellanic Cloud was held back from the previous wave because it read as a veil and cost five times the frame time of the older map. It is not a flat disc: its young stars are measured to stretch over more than {n1} to {n2} kiloparsecs along our line of sight, with the eastern side up to {n3} kiloparsecs nearer than the western. How far each drawn star is in front or behind is a statistical spread round those trends, never a parallax. The Magellanic Bridge and the Stream are neutral hydrogen from a radio survey (HI4PI); only the end at the Clouds is anchored, so the Stream's distance beyond them is a model, and the map says it.
